SECTION C – PROGRAM DESCRIPTION
1 Overview and Authorizing Statutes and Regulations
The U.S. Department of Transportation’s (USDOT) Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
(FMCSA) announces the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 Crash Causal Factors Program (CCFP) Notice
of Funding Opportunity (NOFO), Funding Opportunity Number FM-CCFP-27-001, to solicit
applications from eligible entities to support the Crash Causal Factors Program.
The CCFP is authorized by section 23006(b) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA,
Public Law Number 117-58) and the source of the funding is from P.L. 116-200, “Consolidated
Appropriations Act, 2021”. For FY 2027, FMCSA anticipates awarding up to $7,000,000 to
entities identified further in this document, with an award ceiling of up to $500,000 per award.
Final funding amounts are subject to the availability of funds appropriated by Congress.
2 Crash Causal Factors Program Cooperative Agreement
Program Goals and Objectives
The CCFP is part of the USDOT and FMCSA’s heightened effort to reduce roadway fatalities
involving commercial motor vehicles (CMVs). P.L. 116-200 makes available $30M for FMCSA
to study the cause of large truck crashes while section 23006(b)(1) of the Infrastructure
Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA, Public Law Number 117-58) requires the Secretary to “carry out
a comprehensive study to determine the causes of, and contributing factors to, crashes that
involve a commercial motor vehicle.” To reconcile the differences in IIJA and P.L. 116-200,
FMCSA developed the Crash Causal Factors Program (CCFP), FMCSA’s initiative to better
understand the causal factors in crashes involving CMVs and provide resources to inform safety
programs and crash countermeasures. The CCFP is establishing a framework to compile crash
data that States and local jurisdictions already collect in a national database. This data,
combined with supplemental data needed to answer specific research questions, will support a
series of in-depth CCFP studies and ongoing ad hoc analysis conducted by FMCSA, State/local
partners, and other entities.
The CCFP expands on the original Large Truck Crash Causation Study (LTCCS) that
investigated nearly 1,000 injury-causing and fatal crashes involving large trucks from 2001 to
2003. In the two decades since the LTCCS concluded, the motor carrier industry has grown
significantly, and the transportation sector has seen extensive changes in available technology,
vehicle safety features, driver behaviors, and roadway design.
The goal of the CCFP is to provide nuanced, updated insight into the factors that contribute to
crashes involving CMVs—taking into account the many changes that have occurred since the
original study was completed over 20 years ago—and to empower stakeholders to refine their
safety programs and activities and ultimately reduce crashes. To do so, the program will carry
out a series of peer-reviewed studies that focus on specific vehicle types and crash severities.
It will make the anonymized datasets available to stakeholders while also carrying out analysis
and producing an analytical report. In addition to the studies, the CCFP will establish a
foundation for continued data collection and ad hoc analysis through a database, dashboards,
and other resources.

Success depends on the participation of State and local jurisdiction partners who will be asked
to collect much of the crash data and submit it to the CCFP database. The program strives to
streamline data collection activities, creating an efficient, cost-effective program that can sustain
subsequent studies. To prepare effectively, the team previously asked FMCSA Divisions, States,
and local jurisdiction agencies to complete a series of surveys regarding existing crash response
and data collection processes. Engaging these groups at an early stage and fostering a sense
of collaboration and joint ownership will help ensure the program is successful.
Ultimately, advances in safety are the main impetus for the CCFP. The CCFP aims to produce
scientific, trustworthy resources and analysis that will drive further research and help optimize
safety programs. The program needs to reach groups that can leverage the data and insights to
carry out activities that improve safety. These include government agencies, safety advocacy
groups, research institutions, and other entities interested in using crash data to make decisions
and drive the development of countermeasures.
This NOFO provides important information about the CCFP’s national priorities and highlights
the critical required information needed to prepare and submit an application.
3 CCFP Award Performance Goals
FMCSA will measure whether CCFP Cooperative Agreement applications meet the performance
goals outlined in the application by assessing performance indicators specified in the application.
Applicants should additionally specify performance indicators related to how they will achieve
activities such as:
• Gathering and reporting data from qualifying States.
• Conducting post-crash inspections of CMVs involved in qualifying crashes.
• Conducting post-crash investigations and/or reconstructions of CMVs involved in
qualifying crashes.
4 CCFP Funding Activity Descriptions
This section discusses eligible funding opportunities for the CCFP Cooperative Agreement
Program. Applicants are encouraged to describe how their proposed project addresses one or
more of these funding opportunities.
The CCFP will incorporate data that is already being collected by States and local jurisdictions,
rather than engaging contracted crash data collectors to respond to the scene and collect data
independently. This approach:
• Reduces duplicate efforts at the crash scene, avoiding congestion at the crash scene and
lowering the cost of carrying out studies.
• Minimizes the impact on States by aligning closely with existing procedures.
• Benefits from the expertise and experience of trained professionals, ensuring more
authoritative, higher quality data.
• Creates opportunity for greater value from the data already being collected.

Page | 10
• Provides CMV-specific data that is often excluded from crash studies, allowing analysts
to answer research questions that are important for regulatory, enforcement, and
programmatic considerations.
The CCFP will execute a study, focusing on a specific CMV population. This phase of the
program, the Heavy-Duty Truck Study, will establish a foundation for potential future phases.
This peer-reviewed study will collect and analyze a nationally representative sample of crash
data. Importantly, data protection measures will be in place to protect drivers, motor carriers,
and others who may be contacted by officials for information following a crash. The study data
will be used only for research purposes, and any data that is made publicly available will be
anonymized.
The Heavy-Duty Truck Study aims specifically to better understand fatal crashes involving Class
7/8 trucks (heavy-duty trucks) in the United States. The study data as well as the analytical report
that will be produced at the close of the study are intended to help inform policy and regulations,
safety programs, and activities carried out by safety advocacy groups, CMV industry groups,
motor carriers, drivers, and the public, ultimately to improve safety for everyone and prevent
crashes. Researchers and commercial entities may also be able to leverage the data and
insights to enhance their understanding of crashes and develop effective prevention tools and
strategies.
During the data collection period, cooperation from motor carriers, drivers, and other parties
involved in qualifying crashes will be critical to ensure the study collects accurate, complete, and
thorough data.

support of CCFP Program Goals and Objectives. In describing their proposed projects,
applicants should follow the Project Narrative Requirements in Section D(1.2).

within the sample jurisdictions. The funding aims to enhance

thorough CMV crash investigations and advanced data
collection.
The activity under this section should not include basic

basic State-required police crash reports (PCRs).

Use of funds for this activity includes but is not limited to:

4.2 Funding Considerations
Routine expenses, such as vehicles and operational expenses, should be supported under a
State’s MCSAP formula grant awarded to a MCSAP lead agency and generally will not be
considered under the CCFP program. However, States are eligible to request equipment and
related expenses to supplement their support of CCFP projects if they can clearly demonstrate
a necessity beyond their current MCSAP allocation.
Participating local governments (see Section B, Eligibility Information) are eligible to request
equipment and related expenses to supplement their support of the CCFP projects listed in this
NOFO.
Applicants should refer to the CCFP Cooperative Agreement Cost Eligibility document in
Appendix C for guidance on eligible projects and costs.

Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Public Law Number 117-58 (2021). The CCFP was

from a nationally representative sample of 30 States and local jurisdictions. This program

The budget narrative explains the “what,” “how,” and “why” of each line-item cost to carry out

component that supports the costs of the proposed work and should describe why each budget
item is required to achieve the proposed project goals and objectives. It should also explain in
detail how budget costs were calculated to support the cost being reasonable and allocable.
The budget narrative should be clear, specific, detailed, and mathematically correct. Be sure to

Subject: Crash Causal Factors Program (CCFP) Cooperative Agreement Program:
Justification for Non-Competitive Announcement
SUMMARY
The purpose of this memo is to provide information on why the Federal Motor Carrier Safety
Administration (FMCSA) is choosing to announce the Crash Causal Factors Program (CCFP)
Cooperative Agreement Program non-competitively. This memo provides (1) a brief synopsis of
the program, (2) justification for choosing to announce the CCFP Cooperative Agreement
Program non-competitively, and (3) details as to why the 30 States listed in the CCFP
Cooperative Agreement Program Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) were pre-selected.
PROGRAM SYNOPSIS
Section 23006(b)(1) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA, Public Law Number
117-58) requires the Secretary to “carry out a comprehensive study to determine the causes of,
and contributing factors to, crashes that involve a commercial motor vehicle.” In 2023, FMCSA
launched the CCFP, FMCSA’s initiative to better understand the causal factors in crashes
involving commercial motor vehicles (CMVs) and provide resources to inform safety programs
and crash countermeasures, in accordance with section 23006 of the IIJA.
The CCFP will execute a robust study of crash causal factors, focusing on fatal crashes involving
Class 7/8 trucks (i.e., the Heavy-Duty Truck Study). This peer-reviewed study will collect and
analyze a nationally representative sample of crash data from a select group of States and local
jurisdictions. To accomplish this study, the CCFP is establishing a framework to (1) compile
crash data that States and local jurisdictions already collect, and (2) collect supplemental crash
data to answer specific research questions for the Heavy-Duty Truck Study. This requires

2
Page | 2
extensive collaboration, coordination, and partnership with selected States and jurisdictions.
Because the study requires additional investigative activities and reporting processes that
participating entities may not routinely conduct, the CCFP is establishing the CCFP Cooperative
Agreement Program, to provide funding for qualifying activities and equipment.
JUSTIFICATION FOR NON-COMPETITIVE ANNOUNCEMENT
The CCFP is authorized by section 23006(b) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA,
Public Law Number 117-58). There is limited funding available to support the conduct of this
study; as such, funding under this Cooperative Agreement Program is limited and FMCSA
cannot accept grant applications from States that are not included in the study sample design. For
FY 2027, FMCSA anticipates awarding approximately $7,000,000 to entities identified further in
this document, with an award ceiling of up to $500,000.00 per award. Details as to why the 30
States listed in the CCFP Cooperative Agreement Program NOFO were pre-selected are
provided below.
STATE PRE-SELECTION CRITERIA AND PROCESSES
The CCFP is conducting the Heavy-Duty Truck Study to gain insights on the factors that
contribute to fatal crashes involving Class 7/8 trucks. Study findings will help inform policy and
regulations, safety programs, and activities carried out by safety advocacy groups, CMV industry
groups, motor carriers, drivers, and the public, ultimately to improve safety for everyone and
prevent crashes. To produce scientifically valid, generalizable results, the study must collect and
analyze data from a nationally representative sample of crashes. For this study, FMCSA aims to
collect an annual sample of 1,000 fatal crashes (roughly 25% of the population size) for two
years for a total of 2,000 fatal crashes. This sample of 2,000 fatal crashes will be collected from
sample State and local jurisdictions that have been identified to participate in the study to ensure
national representation while minimizing the burden of participation.
In pursuit of a nationally representative sample, while minimizing the participant burden,
FMCSA selected jurisdictions based on three study criteria outlined below. The use of
randomized sampling to minimize sample bias was not practical due to various aspects of the
study, most importantly the limited size of the study population (2,000 fatal crashes involving
heavy-duty trucks) and resource limitations.
Study Criteria
1. Geographic Diversity. Jurisdiction’s location helps ensure geographic diversity of sample.
2. Investigative Capability. Jurisdiction collects comprehensive data on each crash to support
detailed analysis.
3. Crash Frequency. Jurisdiction’s investigation of fatal crashes involving heavy-duty trucks
contributes to a target of 833 crashes per region to help meet the sample size.
Statistical Methodology for Stratification and Sample Selection
The following sections detail how FMCSA quantified the criteria to select the nationally
representative sample of 30 States.

1. Geographic Diversity

variability, FMCSA stratified the sample by geographic region, as shown in Figure 1. FMCSA

region would be approximately equal. Based on this historical data, Alaska and Hawaii were
excluded from study consideration due to their low number of fatal crashes involving heavy-duty

3. Crash Frequency
FMCSA selected a sample size and then used crash frequency to determine how many States
from each region were needed to achieve a nationally representative sample of 2,000 fatal
crashes.
Selecting a Sample Size
The Heavy-Duty Truck Study builds on the original Large Truck Crash Causation Study
(LTCCS), conducted from 2001–2003, and provides a larger sample size for more reliable,
representative results. The LTCCS total sample involved 967 crashes, which included 1,127
large trucks, 959 non-truck motor vehicles, 251 fatalities, and 1,408 injuries. Of the 1,127 large
trucks involved in crashes that were part of the study, only 62.2% were tractors pulling a semi-
trailer. Similarly, the study included 251 fatalities, which means at most, only 251 fatal crashes
were included in the study, and it’s possible that not all of them involved heavy-duty trucks.
To analyze the factors contributing to fatal crashes involving heavy-duty trucks, the Agency
needs a sample size much larger than 251 fatalities. The Heavy-Duty Truck Study plans to
double the sample size of LTCCS and collect data from at least 2,000 fatal crashes involving
heavy-duty trucks over a period of two years. FMCSA selected the sample size based on a power
analysis which indicated that increasing the sample size significantly beyond 2,000 fatal crashes
would not provide sufficient additional benefits to justify the additional costs.
Applying a Safety Margin to Contextualize Crash Frequency
To identify the target number of crashes needed for each region to ensure the collection of at
least 2,000 fatal crashes, FMCSA developed a safety margin, or multiplier, of 1.667. This margin
is based on historical crash data and findings from the information collection surveys.2 In
particular, the safety margin accounts for the following findings and considerations:
1. Not all crashes that occur within a State are investigated by the State; some are investigated
by local jurisdictions.
2. Not all crashes in a selected area are thoroughly investigated.
3. The national frequency of crashes may decrease by the start of the data collection period.
2 Commercial Motor Vehicle (CMV) Crash Causal Factors Study: Knowledge of Systems and Processes” (OMB Control No. 2126-0079).

Applying this multiplier of 1.667 indicates that the study should target 3,333 fatal crashes over
the course of two years (approximately 833 crashes per region), to ensure the collection of at
least 2,000 fatal crashes.
Assessing Crash Frequency
Once the target of 833 fatal crashes per region was established, FMCSA assessed each State’s
crash frequency by reviewing historical crash data from NHTSA’s FARS (2020-2021). States
with fewer than 12 crashes in 2020-2021 (6 per year on average) were excluded from sample.

CONCLUSION
The CCFP Heavy-Duty Truck Study developed a nationally representative study sample design
using the criteria and processes described above. The study sample design was peer-reviewed
internally by FMCSA subject matter experts and by an external panel of experts. FMCSA is
committed to ensuring the Heavy-Duty Truck Study yields scientifically valid, nationally
representative findings, using the study sample design as a foundational framework. By
collecting data on at least 2,000 fatal crashes involving Class 7/8 large trucks in the 30 States
identified for study participation, FMCSA will have sufficient data to (1) gain critical insights on
the factors that contribute to these crashes, and (2) develop and implement plans to address these
factors, in partnership with the States, industry, and other organizations.
